items.q: A count X can be 0, 1, 2, and so on. Which inequality says "X is at least 3"?

options: That is "more than 3", which leaves out 3.
Right: "at least 3" means 3 or more, so 3 itself is included.

items.q: For a count X, which is the same as "fewer than 3"?

why.correct: "Fewer than 3" means $X < 3$. For counts, the largest such value is 2, so it is $X \le 2$. Reading it as $X \le 3$ is a classic slip.
options: That is "at least 3", the opposite group of counts.
That leaves out 2, which is fewer than 3.
Right: fewer than 3 is $X < 3$, and for whole-number counts that is 0, 1 or 2, so $X \le 2$.

items.q: A count X can be 0 to 6. Which values are included in "at most 2"? Select all that apply.

options: Right: at most 2 includes every count up to and including 2.

items.q: Out of 10 free throws, a player makes "more than 4". For the count X of free throws made, which inequality fits?

why.correct: "More than 4" is $X > 4$, which for counts is $X \ge 5$.
options: Right: more than 4 is $X > 4$, which for whole numbers is 5 or more.
That includes 4, but "more than 4" does not.
That leaves out 5, which is more than 4.

why.correct: "No more than 5" is the same as "at most 5": $X \le 5$.
options: That leaves out 5, which "no more than 5" allows.
That is "at least 5", the opposite direction.
Right: no more than 5 means 5 or fewer.

items.q: A count X can be 0, 1, 2, ... , 8. Which counts make up "at least one"?

why.correct: "At least one" is $X \ge 1$: every value except 0. It is often easiest to find by starting with all the values and removing 0.
options: Right: "at least one" is every count except 0.
That is "more than one", which leaves out 1.
Right: inclusive means both ends are included.
That describes the values outside the range.

items.q: Which phrase means the same as $X \ge 3$?

why.correct: "No fewer than 3" and "at least 3" both mean $X \ge 3$.
options: Right: not fewer than 3 means 3 or more.

items.q: Ten students read 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 9 books. How many students read at least 5 books?

why.correct: "At least 5" includes 5: the students with 5, 6 and 9 books, so 3 students.
options: That counts only 6 and 9, leaving out the student who read exactly 5.
Right: the counts 5, 6 and 9 are 5 or more.
That also counts the student who read 4, which is fewer than 5.
5 is the boundary value, not the number of students.

items.q: For a count, "fewer than 3" and "3 or fewer" give different answers. For a commute time measured very precisely, do "less than 20 minutes" and "20 minutes or less" give very different proportions?

why.correct: For counts the boundary value matters a lot ($X < 3$ is $X \le 2$). For continuous measurements, including or leaving out the exact boundary barely changes anything.
options: Right: for a continuous variable the boundary itself holds almost no values, so the two proportions are nearly equal.
True in words, but for a precise measurement that is almost no one.
The two phrases differ only at the boundary, not by half the data.
Commute times are measurements (continuous), not counts.
No: almost no one has a commute of exactly 20.000 minutes
Yes: "or less" adds each commute of exactly 20 minutes
Yes: one of them leaves out half of the data
No: commute times are counts, so the phrases agree

items.q: For a count X from 0 to 10, put these events in order from the fewest included values to the most.

why.correct: Exactly 4 is one value; fewer than 4 is 0 to 3 (four values); at most 4 is 0 to 4 (five values); at least 4 is 4 to 10 (seven values).
